notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The course introduces students to the linguistic diversity of French‑speaking Africa with a special focus on Bantu languages. It explores the historical and linguistic landscape, indigenous languages, colonial legacies, major structural features—phonology, morphology, and syntax. It also examines how centuries of multilingualism and contact with French have shaped language use across the region. Through case studies, students analyze patterns of language change, borrowing, and code‑switching, language and media, as well as the sociopolitical and cultural forces that influence language policy, identity, and everyday communication.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - Food and Media This course explores the ever-growing significance of food studies within the discipline of media studies. From bartering over food to the use of lavish dinners to symbolize opulence and status, humans have used food – its preparation, its ingredients, its consumption – as a means to communicate their position within society and their understanding of its values. As our relationship with food becomes increasingly mediated, food as an indispensable part of human existence has become a reflection of our society at large. This class will examine the history of food production as represented in print media (e.g. recipe books, newspapers and advertisements) and other media forms, including food photography, cooking shows, and social media. We will examine a wide range of socio-cultural issues, including health and dieting, class and labor, gender and sexuality, race and diaspora, and the commercialization of food-related content in diverse forms of media. LEC0201 - The Devil This course examines the Devil as a dynamic and evolving presence across religious texts and media forms from antiquity to the present day, examining his prominent role in medieval Christianity and early modern debates shaped by witch trials and the Reformation. It explores the Victorian shift toward a more sympathetic and rebellious adversary, influenced by writers like John Milton and William Blake, and continues into modern reinterpretations in literature, film, TV, and digital media. Drawing on key literature and immersive lectures, this course explores how evolving religious and media contexts have shaped the world’s first influencer into one of the most enduring and provocative forces in history. BMS301H1S LEC0201 is cross-listed with CHC300H1S LEC0101. Students cannot take both courses for credit.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - Media in Transition: AI Chatbots, Ethics, and the Law This course examines the history of social AI as an emergent media form and focuses on the rapid deployment and impact of Generative AI Chatbots as virtual companions, writing partners, therapists, and as grief technologies such as ghostbots. The course will foreground ethical, sociocultural, ecomedia, and legal issues arising from these rapidly evolving sociotechnologies. As a seminar, team collaboration on in-class testing of GenAI and presentations will address topics such as emotional inequality, algorithmic bias, attention hacking, privacy by design, age appropriate design, surveillance and platform capitalism. Key scholarly and critical work, theoretical models, legal arguments, and case studies will contextualize the benefits and the dangers of intimate interactions with personalized, always-on chatbots within existing and proposed regulatory frameworks in the EU, UK, US and Canada.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC5101 - Aldus Manutius and the rise of the modern book This advanced seminar explores Aldus Manutius’ impact on Renaissance print culture and the modern book. As a scholar and knowledge gatekeeper, he pioneered the octavo format, italic type, and classical editions, shaping the rising publishing industry. Through primary source analysis and hands-on experiential learning activities at Kelly Library, Trinity College Library and Fisher Library, students will engage with early printed books and incunabula, including Hypnerotomachia Poliphili and Aldine editions.

courses.name: Advanced Open Topics in Book & Media Studies

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - The Book Remixed This course examines the phenomenon of books that have been created from the physical materials of other, pre-existing books. Students will engage with the fact of that making and remix and the various interpretations that it can encourage. They will explore books that remix other books with gusto and often themselves along the way. Books that ask to be shuffled. Books shredded and rewoven. Books erased and redrawn, books printed on film, books of made-up scripts exploded as a gallery installation. The primary focus of the course will be on books of the 20th and 21st centuries and will include a visit or two to rare book collections on campus. Assignments will include creative exercises, class presentations, and a critical analysis of the prosody and poetics of a chosen book. Note that participation will weigh heavily in assessment and that students will be required to purchase a number of texts in hardcopy. LEC5101 - World Calligraphy: History, Scripts, and Practice This course offers an advanced study of world calligraphy as a material and cultural practice central to the history of the book and visual communication. The first part of the course surveys the historical development of major calligraphic traditions and script families across world writing systems, including Latin majuscule and minuscule hands, Arabic naskh and thuluth, East Asian brush scripts (zhuàn shū and kǎi shū), Hebrew square and cursive scripts, and Devanagari. Attention is given to the aesthetic and functional evolution of letterforms within their respective cultural contexts. The second part of the course adopts an experiential learning approach. Through sustained studio practice, students acquire foundational competence in selected scripts, developing skills in pen angle, brush control, stroke sequence, spacing, and compositional layout. Prior experience in calligraphy is not required, but a predisposition toward writing and the manual arts is recommended.

Assignments will include creative exercises, class presentations, and a critical analysis of the prosody and poetics of a chosen book. Note that participation will weigh heavily in assessment and that students will be required to purchase a number of texts in hardcopy. 

LEC5101 - World Calligraphy: History, Scripts, and Practice 

This course offers an advanced study of world calligraphy as a material and cultural practice central to the history of the book and visual communication. The first part of the course surveys the historical development of major calligraphic traditions and script families across world writing systems, including Latin majuscule and minuscule hands, Arabic naskh and thuluth, East Asian brush scripts (zhuàn shū and kǎi shū), Hebrew square and cursive scripts, and Devanagari. Attention is given to the aesthetic and functional evolution of letterforms within their respective cultural contexts. The second part of the course adopts an experiential learning approach. Through sustained studio practice, students acquire foundational competence in selected scripts, developing skills in pen angle, brush control, stroke sequence, spacing, and compositional layout. Prior experience in calligraphy is not required, but a predisposition toward writing and the manual arts is recommended.

courses.name: Introduction to Critical Issues in Caribbean Health

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course examines mental health in Caribbean and Caribbean diasporic contexts through an interdisciplinary lens that integrates psychological science, public health, and social justice frameworks. It explores how colonial histories, racialized knowledge systems, and structural inequities shape mental health outcomes, while engaging critically with clinical models, health data, and service delivery systems. Students will be introduced to key concepts in mental health, including diagnostic frameworks, epidemiology, and health system design, and will analyze how these “STEM” dimensions intersect with culture, power, and access. Particular attention will be paid to the experiences of Black Caribbean populations, including the impacts of migration, gender, and socio-economic inequality on mental health and well-being. The course moves beyond critique to examine how mental health systems operate in practice, including access to care, digital health technologies, and policy frameworks. Students will be encouraged to think critically about what counts as valid knowledge in health, and how alternative and community-based approaches to healing can challenge dominant paradigms. Through a combination of lectures, discussions, and applied assignments, students will develop the ability to connect scientific knowledge with social realities and to propose more equitable approaches to mental health care.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - The Devil This course examines the Devil as a dynamic and evolving presence across religious texts and media forms from antiquity to the present day, examining his prominent role in medieval Christianity and early modern debates shaped by witch trials and the Reformation. It explores the Victorian shift toward a more sympathetic and rebellious adversary, influenced by writers like John Milton and William Blake, and continues into modern reinterpretations in literature, film, TV, and digital media. Drawing on key literature and immersive lectures, this course explores how evolving religious and media contexts have shaped the world’s first influencer into one of the most enduring and provocative forces in history. CHC300H1S LEC0101 is cross-listed with BMS301H1S LEC0201. Students cannot take both courses for credit.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions How do we know if a justice policy works? Can we prove that interventions reduce crime or that new reforms protect rights better than the old ones? In this course, we dive into the world of social experiments and evidence-based research to explore how data is used to test and sometimes challenge assumptions about the justice system. You'll learn how real-world studies are designed to make causal claims, how to tell if the evidence is convincing, and how to evaluate the numbers behind headlines and policy briefs critically. This is a hands-on, discussion-driven class that gives you the statistical foundation to understand (and question) how decisions in the justice system are made. No software skills required—just your curiosity and willingness to think critically. By the end of the course, you’ll be able to spot flawed research, understand how experiments and surveys shape policy, and build a solid foundation in statistical reasoning, skills that are essential for anyone thinking about research, policy, or law school.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions What does justice look like outside the courtroom? This course examines the wide range of adjudicative, investigative, and oversight bodies that operate alongside, and sometimes in place of, the courts. From coroner's inquests and public inquiries, to special investigation units, human rights tribunals, consent and capacity boards, and even university tribunals, these diverse bodies exercise both quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative powers to adjudicate individual claims, investigate institutional conduct, produce official records of contested events, and recommend reform. Through case studies examining investigations of police use-of-force, inquiries into violence against Indigenous women, girls, and two-spirit people, and others students will examine the historical development and contemporary practice of these processes. Together, we will think critically about the architecture of public decision-making in Canada and beyond and the different conceptions of justice that emerge when law operates beyond the courts.

What does justice look like outside the courtroom? This course examines the wide range of adjudicative, investigative, and oversight bodies that operate alongside, and sometimes in place of, the courts. From coroner's inquests and public inquiries, to special investigation units, human rights tribunals, consent and capacity boards, and even university tribunals, these diverse bodies exercise both quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative powers to adjudicate individual claims, investigate institutional conduct, produce official records of contested events, and recommend reform. Through case studies examining investigations of police use-of-force, inquiries into violence against Indigenous women, girls, and two-spirit people, and others students will examine the historical development and contemporary practice of these processes. Together, we will think critically about the architecture of public decision-making in Canada and beyond and the different conceptions of justice that emerge when law operates beyond the courts.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course examines the multifaceted role of religion within the criminal justice system. It explores how religious beliefs and communities shape criminal behaviour, moral regulation, and desistance. It analyses the interaction between religion and law through legal pluralism and landmark Canadian cases, as well as the historical theological foundations of concepts like reasonable doubt. The course addresses contemporary issues, including religiously motivated hate crime, the influence of police officers’ personal religiosity, and the roles of chaplaincy and faith-based organizations in policing and corrections. Concluding with perspectives from public theology, the course considers how concepts such as mercy, restoration, and forgiveness can inform more inclusive and effective approaches to justice.

notes.text: Timetable Instructions Digital Feminisms investigates the complex layering of identities in and through digital technology, tools, and data. Assignments encourage us to put feminist methods into practice through critical creation and analysis of digital tools, designing an anti-racist/feminist/queer prototype, and creating our own zine.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101: Artificial Intelligence, Literature and Culture This class will examine literary representations and cultural impacts of artificial intelligence (AI), broadly conceived. The second half of the class will focus on the implications of Artificial Intelligence as both tools to assist, and rivals of, human writers. Through hands-on experience using AI tools, students will gain crucial media literacy skills while also thinking critically about AI’s actual and potential applications. Reading literary representations of and by AI will allow us to grapple with the ethical and aesthetic questions raised by such texts: are there unique human qualities and activities, or can/will AI replicate every facet of humanity? What ethical responsibilities do humans owe to AI? What do we want from AI? What does it mean when AI begins writing convincingly? By looking at the past and present representations and implications of AI while, also experimenting with contemporary AI tools, we consider if and how AI might be productively incorporated into our lives in a way that maintains our intellectual and creative autonomy. LEC0201: Decolonial Digital Humanities Digital Humanities has contributed important conceptual and practical insights at the intersection of digital technologies and the humanities but hasn’t always sufficiently recognized the colonial implications of the technologies and tools they work with, nor with non-Western perspectives on and engagements with digital technologies. This course addresses this gap by examining the ways technology and digital media have perpetuated colonial ideologies and power structures as well as the ways Indigenous and decolonial approaches to digital technology and tools can inform digital projects that challenge colonial structures and support decolonization efforts of Indigenous cultures, communities, and nations. This seminar course will center flexible opportunities for student-led learning and discussion alongside work on creative digital projects that directly address course themes and concepts.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101: The Secret Renaissance What is the opposite of the Mona Lisa? Of the Sistine Chapel? Of Bruegel’s winter scenes? This course will explore lesser-known works of art produced in Europe during the Renaissance that shaped culture at that time. Beyond just learning about paintings and sculpture, this course will examine “fringe” objects, such as Sicilian Tests di Moro,” Netherlandish “witch-soul daggers,” and wax divination hands. This class will explore how the art and objects made by marginalized groups in the Renaissance became integral aspects of mainstream Renaissance culture and helped inform our contemporary understanding of life in Renaissance Europe. It will dive into aspects of the occult and “pseudo-religion” examining how those outside of conventual religion influenced everyday life in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, all while going unnoticed by the authorities. This course will make you rethink what you think you know about European Renaissance art and culture. LEC0201: Art and Architecture of the Eastern Roman Provinces How did a single empire hold together dozens of peoples stretching from Spain to Arabia? At the Sebasteion in Aphrodisias, in western Türkiye, a remarkable series of reliefs personifies up to 50 of the Roman empire's subject peoples—a vivid testament to the ancient world's diversity and the imperial power that bound it. This course investigates the art and architecture of the eastern Roman provinces from the 2nd century BCE to the 6th century CE. Examining monuments and sculpture from Greece, Türkiye, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Syria, and Egypt, we trace the exercise of imperial violence, the endurance of local traditions, and the ties between modern imperialism and ancient heritage—from the dispersal of Palmyrene grave monuments to museums worldwide to the recent destruction at Palmyra, ending with the founding of Constantinople. LEC0301: The History of Art and Crime This course examines the fascinating and complex world of art crime, exploring its role in a range of topics including theft, forgery, trafficking, looting, vandalism, appropriation, and white-collar infractions. Through the study of cases from antiquity to the recent 2025 Louvre heist, it investigates the underbelly of the art ecosystem as well as the motivations and methods of its criminals. Turning students into sleuths, classes offer a counter-narrative to conventional art history and investigate the legal, ethical, and social complexities of protecting cultural heritage by following its stories beyond galleries into courtrooms and criminal investigations. Through the consideration of art crimes not only as a form of unlawful activity, but also as a lens through which to understand the economics and power of cultural output, the class ultimately asks: What and who has the ability to determine art's authenticity, value, ownership and place in history?

notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course examines drawing by artists and architects in early modern Europe (c. 1500–1800), from artistic to technical drawing, as both an object of study and a working practice. Students will study how drawing came to be understood as a category in its own right— moving from a workshop tool to an object of collecting and connoisseurship — and what this shift reveals about changing perceptions of drawing, then and since. The course will also introduce students to professionals who work with drawings today, including curators, dealers, and connoisseurs, through guest presentations and discussion, and will include at least one visit to a local collection to study original drawings firsthand.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The course instructor will confirm the room prior to the start of classes. LEC0101 Textiles of the Indian Ocean World Many of the world’s great textile arts -- from colourful printed cottons to complex silks --emerged within the Indian Ocean world, a shared maritime space which stretches from eastern Africa to Southern China. Using the ROM’s extensive collections, this course will survey the wide variety of Indian Ocean textile arts--their fibres, techniques, dyes, design and iconography, as well as their deep social and political meanings. Special attention is given to the traditions of South and Southeast Asia and Madagascar. Students will further engage with the variety of conceptual framings used today to situate textiles within aesthetic and social worlds. In this experiential course, students will hone skills in slow reading of objects, and learn how exhibitions are made as the ROM prepares to open “Monsoon Worlds of the Indian Ocean” in April 2027. LEC0201 Introduction to Contemporary African and African Diasporic Art Theories This introductory course examines key theories and the social-political moments that have informed Contemporary African and African Diasporic art. The course will challenge and complicate the idea of Africa, by exploring issues of migration, creolization and liberation. The large-scale textile work of French-Caribbean artist Raphaël Barontini, installed at the ROM (September 2026 to August 2027), will be a source and focal point for the course. As such, classes will be held at the ROM for direct engagement with Barontini's work and with ROM's Global Africa historical collections. Barontini critically engages museum collections and archives, intentionally engaging with gaps, omissions and histories of political resistance to amplify underrepresented narratives. Centred on figuration, his work includes a wide range of mediums including painting, printmaking, costume design, and performance. The course will explore the politics of these mediums from a colonial times to present day. This course will examine how Barontini and his contemporaries can be read alongside texts by Okwui Enwezor, Saidiya Hartmann, Achille Mbembe, Dan Hicks, Édouard Glissant, Francoise Verges and the several others to think about Africa in relation to the Encyclopedic museum as well as African rooted art historical continuums.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions An introduction to the French tradition of cultural studies through key French thinkers on culture and history, drawing on figures such as Roland Barthes, Michel Foucault, Pierre Bourdieu, Louis Althusser, Julia Kristeva, Jacques Derrida, and Gilles Deleuze. By situating French critical theory within a broader framework of intellectual history and focusing on the emergence of (post)modern subjectivity and cultural production, the course provides students with access to the philosophical and theoretical debates that continue to shape the Humanities today. The rise of Cultural Studies in North America was influenced by an increasing interest in popular culture, the impact of the British school of Cultural Studies, and the reception of European theory. In addition, postcolonial studies and debates surrounding postmodernity have become central to contemporary approaches to culture, encompassing a wide range of media—including literature, film, and digital culture—as well as socio-political and anthropological studies of communities. This course focuses particularly on the European—and especially French—contribution to this intellectual paradigm by examining its historical development, cultural context, ideological assumptions, and theoretical foundations. Students will have the opportunity to work both collaboratively and independently with a wide range of cultural materials. Students who are proficient in French and intend to complete their readings and major assignments in French in order for this course to count toward a program in French should inform the Course Instructor of their decision prior to submission of the first assignment.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The course is taught in English . Delivery Instructions Why did Walmart’s attempt to break into the German market go down in flames? What factors have turned soccer clubs like Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund into global brands? How has globalization impacted traditional German culture and what is unique about the German and European experience of globalization? The course explores the contemporary character of globalization patterns and problems in German contexts and prepares students for future academic and professional opportunities in Germany and beyond. The course is highly recommended as preparation for students interested in participating in iPRAKTIKUM , the Department of German’s internationalization and experiential Learning program, which provides exciting placements in Germany and the GTA. It also fulfills a requirement for the U of T’s Global Scholar Certificate .

Why did Walmart’s attempt to break into the German market go down in flames? What factors have turned soccer clubs like Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund into global brands? How has globalization impacted traditional German culture and what is unique about the German and European experience of globalization?

The course explores the contemporary character of globalization patterns and problems in German contexts and prepares students for future academic and professional opportunities in Germany and beyond. The course is highly recommended as preparation for students interested in participating in iPRAKTIKUM, the Department of German’s internationalization and experiential Learning program, which provides exciting placements in Germany and the GTA. It also fulfills a requirement for the U of T’s Global Scholar Certificate.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course is taught in English. What does it mean to grow up in a nation constantly redefining its own borders, history, and identity? This course explores the German Bildungsroman in cinema – the traditional coming-of-age film – through the lens of 20th and 21st-century cinematic works. Moving across four thematic modules, we will examine how filmmakers have used figures of youth to navigate Germany’s complex historical fractures and contemporary social realities.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Cities, or at least parts of cities, have long been framed as a problem, particularly in large sprawling federalist societies like the United States and Canada. Exactly what those problems are, who they affect, and what should be done (or not done) about them varies over time and space. This is a seminar on the social construction of urban problems. We will explore the tension between on-the-ground challenges such as deprivation, crime, and depopulation, on the one hand, and the way that these problems are deployed by political and economic elites to motivate (or in some cases avoid) change, on the other.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - God and Geometry This course engages controversial issues in the natural sciences of importance to Christian faith, with particular emphases on their ancient and the medieval origins and enactments. Examples include: Harmony vs. Chaos, Creation vs. Evolution, Free Will vs. Determinism, Reason vs. Revelation, Miraculous vs. Natural Causation. LEC0101 is cross-listed with CHC383H1. If you are interested in taking more than one MST301H1S lecture section, please enrol in CHC383H1 in place of LEC0101. CHC383H1S will be used to fulfill program requirements. LEC0201 - The Global Middle Ages The premodern world was an interconnected network of merchandise, luxury goods, religious beliefs, philosophies, and artistic production that celebrated the staples of narrative storytelling, from brave warriors and courtly lovers to tragic histories and comedies of daily life. In this course, we will explore a broad range of medieval literature (all in modern English translation) from around the world: Europe, the Mediterranean world, Africa, and Asia. We will encounter a variety of genres, including epics, sagas, romances, fabliaux, riddles, drama, lyrics, and saints’ lives, and we will work to situate each work in its social and historical contexts with materials from libraries, museums, and art galleries both at home and abroad. LEC0301 - Imagining the World: Maps in the Middle Ages The history of map making, or cartography, often makes a strong distinction between the fantastical accounts of the world in pre-modern maps and the apparently accurate and technical maps of the modern era.  Maps, regardless of what period they are from, are primarily representations of how people regard the world in terms of their cultural and religious values.  In this course, we will explore how people in the Middle Ages mapped out their understanding of reality.  We will start with how they mapped the universe as a whole and then we will move to how the physical world around them was captured in illustrations and literary accounts.  We will extract from these representations the core cultural and religious values that were the engines of map design.  The course will conclude with world maps that were created for trade but also for identifying who was a friend and who was a stranger. LEC0401 - Mystery, Forgery, and Fake News in Medieval and Early Modern Books The history of bookmaking, from antiquity to relatively recent times, is riddled with enigmatic and mesmerizing artifacts—objects that have ignited endless debates and spilled rivers of ink. In some cases, scholars have yet to reach a universally accepted conclusion about their authenticity, their origins, or their meaning. Since control over written culture has always been a powerful tool for advancing political, ideological, and economic interests, it is hardly surprising that forgers in every age have sought to exploit it. In this course, we will come face to face with some of these extraordinary objects and figures: manuscripts, papyri, and maps that have left an indelible mark on the cultural history of Europe—and far beyond. Among them are the Donation of Constantine, a medieval parchment of enormous political consequence—tragically, and spectacularly, a forgery; the Voynich Manuscript, a book shrouded in the mystery of an undeciphered script and an unknown language that has defied every attempt at interpretation; the Vinland Map, a medieval vision of the world astonishingly ahead of its time, on which even the most advanced scientific methods have stumbled (though not philology…); the Artemidorus Papyrus, a precious document whose authenticity continues to spark fierce scholarly battles; and Constantine Simonides, a Greek forger who claimed to possess original manuscripts of Homer and the Bible. We will examine the challenges these haunting artifacts pose to scholars, explore the methods used to unravel—or fail to unravel—their secrets, and reflect more broadly on their significance for the eras in which they were (or were not) created. Ultimately, we will ask what these objects can still teach us about the world we inhabit today.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - Old Saxon Old Saxon is the language spoken by the Continental Saxons--those who did not migrate to Britain in the fifth and sixth centuries. It is closely related to Old English and Old High German, and is one of the oldest surviving Germanic languages. The principal literary monument is the Heliand, a narrative of the life of Christ based on the four gospels of the New Testament, composed in alliterative Germanic metre. This course provides an introduction to the language through reading selections of the Heliand. LEC0201 - Windows into the Workshop: Artists and Art Practice in the Middle Ages & Renaissance In this seminar, we will peer through the window of the workshop to better understand medieval and early modern makers, their work, and the world they inhabited. Practical aspects, such as materials, techniques, and the economics of craft will be considered in conjunction with intellectual and spiritual aspects of making as they relate to concepts of labor, perfection, and the imagination.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - Medieval Deaths and Afterlives Death, dying, and the dead have always been the subject of curiosity and speculation. In the middle ages, the answers were no clearer than they are today. This course explores various medieval conceptions of death and the afterlife. By examining primary source material including medical manuals, saints’ lives, court records, wills, art, visionary accounts, and ghost stories, students will gain an understanding of the ways in which medieval society navigated the inevitability of death and the decay of the physical body, the glories of paradise, and the dead who could not rest.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Description: India is a rising power, the world's fifth largest economy, a nuclear power, and a demographic powerhouse. But it has also has comparatively low literacy levels, high levels of poverty, dropping fertility rates, and an education and health system in crisis. It has fractious relationships in its neighborhood, and a tense relationship with China, but a strong friendship with Russia, as well as a growing partnership with the United States. In short, India is a country of contradictions, and engages in foreign policy behavior that is not only puzzling to other countries - it has stayed studiedly neutral in the Ukraine crisis for example - but is also a challenge for analysis. The goal of this course is to teach how we can identify and understand the puzzling foreign policy behaviors of any country by using India as an example. Designed as a collaborative workshop, this course will teach you to research, analyze and write a paper on the foreign policy behavior of a country of your choice.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Description: This course examines the persistent gap between the formal recognition of Indigenous rights in international and domestic legal frameworks and their implementation in practice. It explores the legal, political, and institutional barriers that shape policy outcomes, including government commitments, judicial interpretations, corporate interests, and grassroots advocacy. Case studies from different jurisdictions will highlight challenges such as Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC), land rights disputes, and self-determination efforts, offering a critical analysis of how political dynamics and legal structures interact to enable or obstruct Indigenous rights realization.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Questions can be directed to undergraduatecoordinator.munkschool@utoronto.ca Description: This course aims to give students the tools necessary to understand legal and policy issues in cyberspace. While it is impossible to become a cybersecurity expert in a single semester, students will leave the course as intelligent laypeople, adept at discussing computer and Internet security policy issues and able to spot political agendas disguised as technical arguments. Students will understand how technology and policy interrelate, when it’s time to turn to technical experts, and how to use technical expertise to form effective policy. This course is designed for policymakers rather than for implementers of preexisting policy. As such, we will not discuss how to implement Internet security policies within government organizations. Rather, we will discuss how to effectively determine which policies are the correct ones to mandate: for government, for private industry, and for individuals. This course is less about learning a body of answers, and more about learning a way of thinking about the topics in general. After completing this class, you will be more sophisticated when you approach new Internet security policy issues. Specifically, you will be able to weigh pros and cons, examine consequences of policies, and craft and recommend policies of your own.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Explore the science of how to cultivate a Happy Mind. This course will merge cutting-edge research from cognitive neuroscience, psychology, and contemplative traditions to investigate what it means to live a fulfilling life. Students will engage with scientific models of well-being, including computational neuroscience models, computational psychiatry, and the neuroscience of emotions. They will study how the mind constructs its reality through predictions, emotions, and habits, examining both the promises and perils of these processes. This course may count towards Breadth Requirement 5: The Physical and Mathematical Universes. If you wish to use this course towards this Breadth Category, please contact your College Registrar's Office to request for it to be manually applied.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Principles of Pharmacogenetics Theory and Practice This course will introduce basic pharmacogenetics concepts and provide opportunity for hands-on practice with the tools used within the field. Through applying genetic concepts, students will use research protocols to: (i) clean genetic data, (ii) use statistical inference to analyze unobserved genotypes, (iii) identify variants of relevance for drug response or unwanted effects of drugs, and (iv) calculate polygenic risk scores. Guest scientists will provide examples of the successful use of pharmacogenetics in the field of personalized medicine. Student inquiries should be directed to the course department: undergrad.pharmtox@utoronto.ca.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The Research Participation course (POL 395H/396H) is a 0.5 credit course for supervised participation in faculty research project. This course is offered only when a faculty member is willing and available to supervise . The interested faculty member review plans with the Undergraduate Director and then make the opportunity known to students as appropriate. The information will be posted on our website https://www.politics.utoronto.ca/undergraduate/curriculum-course-information/research-participation-courses and students can pick up an application form from the undergraduate office. POL 395H/396H is only available to students in their third year of study (i.e., who have completed at least 9.0 credits). The course is like POL 299Y in that it gives undergraduate students an opportunity to engage in research with a faculty member. notes.text: Timetable Instructions Students will be expected to watch asynchronous lecture videos prior to in-person tutorials. Weekly in-person Physiology in Practice classes with professors will take place on Wednesdays from 14:00 to 15:00 at Con Hall. Term tests will be held in person and on campus and will take place Mondays, Wednesdays, or Fridays from 14:00 to 15:00 (Toronto time) on scheduled dates (TBA). Lectures ~3h/week, Physiology in Practice classes 1h/week, and five (5) in-person one (1) hour tutorials per term. The lecture videos will be posted to watch asynchronously. Physiology in Practice classes, tutorials, and tests will run in-person. Delivery Instructions Approx 3 hours of online lecture recordings that can be viewed at any time. 1 hour Physiology in Practice session with the professor 2 to 3 pm at Con Hall in person 5 X 1-hour tutorials with TAs in-person throughout the term. In-person tests and exams. There are two in-person term tests, 50 minutes each generally set for Fridays, but might also be on Mondays or Wednesdays — time 2 to 3 pm. The final in-person assessment will be announced by the Faculty of Arts and Science. Please do not schedule any classes or labs during the test periods, as they will conflict with the Physiology in Practice and testing times. Conflicts will not be accommodated.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions What does AI make visible, what does it render invisible, and whose lives are at stake in the difference? This course introduces students to feminist, anti-racist, and anti-colonial approaches to AI and algorithmic systems. Through cases including facial recognition, automated welfare, hiring technologies, platform recommendations, smart cities, environmental extraction and institutional equity work, students will examine how technologies reproduce and reshape relations of gender, race, class, and colonial power.
